doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Teaching at William Paterson and learning from students
summary: Teaching is learning; he cites Travis Shook's voicing, Coltrane and John Gilmore, and Ahmad Jamal's insistence that everyone needs to practice.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Man you’ve had quite a career. And it’s active now in the education part of it at William Paterson, it added a lot for you?

Right. Yeah, it’s been, because this sounds like a redundant statement but as Ted Dunbar used to say teaching is learning and learning is teaching and it’s true. Because if you get students, especially if you’ve got students who can already play, and you show them something, then they say, “You mean do it like this?” And you say, “Wait a minute, what was that?” Yeah okay. I’ll keep it for myself. So I teach but I also learn. Like I was saying earlier, I played this song, and I said, “Hey Eric, this is what Travis played.” One of Eric’s closest friends, Travis Shook. Wonderful piano player. And I was playing this song of mine and he did a voice of a chord so I still use that voicing that he showed me, all the time. You know Coltrane was like that. He played some stuff, he had some stuff he played where later on in his life he started playing [scats]. He got that from John Gilmore. Of course I was on Birdland on the night when he sat in when John Gilmore, and John Gilmore was sitting in with Pete LaRoca and Trane said, “Woo man” he said, “hey Pete, let John play” because Trane liked it [scats] and Trane put it in print on the next day, he said, “this is something I got from John Gilmore.” I told him, John, that’s the way Trane was. Some guys say well I’ve got my own thing and I got this, and I say, “No you don’t. Everybody’s got something from somebody.” And then you take it and turn it around in a certain way. But no, the teaching area has been good for me because like I said before, I don’t consider myself a teacher, I’m an advanced student. That’s it. Because if you get to the point where you say I know it all, you’re not going to grow. I want to continue to grow. I told Ahmad Jamal something once you know. I knew what he was going to say. I said, “Ahmad, you sound so good, you don’t need to practice.” He said “let me tell you something, Harold Mabern, everybody needs to practice.” And he’s right. And I knew what he was going to say I just wanted — and if he’s at home now he’s got two Steinway D’s up there you see. And so that’s why he’s Ahmad Jamal because he’s not wasting any time. He’s constantly improving and writing more beautiful songs and sounding better on that piano you know.
